problem: Before CI/CD, shipping a change to a production system — a config script, a web app, an infrastructure template — meant a human manually building it, manually testing it, and manually deploying it, usually late at night, usually with a checklist that someone eventually skips a line on. Every manual step is a place where a tired engineer introduces a bug, forgets a step, or deploys the wrong version. The business cost is not abstract: slow release cycles mean features and fixes sit unreleased for weeks, and manual deployment mistakes cause outages at the worst possible time — during business hours, during a trading session, during a client's active support ticket.

For an operation like FundedNext, where the AgentPlatform tool that the CX team depends on every shift is being actively rebuilt (Google Apps Script to Next.js, per the migration blueprint), the business problem is concrete: every time a fix to a broken KYC search or a new calculator tab is ready, someone has to decide — do I paste this code in and pray, or do I have a repeatable, tested, reversible way to get it live? CI/CD is the engineering answer to that question.
concept: CI/CD is two connected disciplines wearing one hyphen. Continuous Integration (CI) is the practice of merging every developer's code changes into a shared branch frequently — multiple times a day — with an automated build and test run on every merge, so integration problems are caught in minutes, not months. Continuous Delivery (CD) extends this: after CI passes, the code is automatically packaged into a deployable artifact and pushed through staging environments, verified, and left ready for a human to approve into production with one click. Continuous Deployment goes one step further and removes even that click — every change that passes all automated gates goes straight to production.

The core idea underneath all three: turn deployment from a rare, risky, manual event into a routine, boring, automated one. Boring is the goal. A deployment pipeline that nobody thinks twice about is a well-built one.
The Three Variants at a Glance Term What Happens After Tests Pass Human Gate?

Continuous Integration Code is merged, built, and automatically tested N/A — this is the build/test stage Continuous Delivery Artifact is built and staged, ready to release Yes — a person clicks "deploy" Continuous Deployment Artifact goes straight to production No — fully automatic
deep: A CI/CD pipeline is a directed graph of stages, each stage a set of jobs, each job a set of steps run on a runner (an ephemeral VM or container). A typical pipeline for a Next.js application like the AgentPlatform rebuild looks like this:
1. Trigger — a git push or pull request against a watched branch fires a webhook to the CI system (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins).
2. Checkout — the runner clones the repository at the exact commit SHA that triggered the run.
3. Install — dependencies are restored, ideally from a lockfile (package-lock.json) and a cache, so npm install is deterministic and fast.
4. Lint & type-check — ESLint and `tsc --noEmit` run to catch style and type errors before anything is built.
5. Unit/integration tests — the test suite runs in an isolated environment; a failure here stops the pipeline immediately (fail fast).
6. Build — `next build` compiles the application into an optimized production artifact.
7. Artifact packaging — the build output is captured (a container image, a Vercel build, a zip) and given an immutable version identifier, usually the commit SHA.
8. Deploy to staging — the artifact is pushed to a non-production environment that mirrors production as closely as possible.
9. Automated verification — smoke tests or health checks confirm the staging deploy is actually working, not just "deployed".
10.Promotion gate — for Continuous Delivery, a human approves; for Continuous Deployment, this step is skipped.
11.Deploy to production — the same artifact (never a rebuild) is promoted to production.
12.Post-deploy checks — health checks, error-rate monitoring, and automatic rollback triggers watch the new version.

The critical engineering principle inside that list is "build once, deploy many": the exact binary/artifact tested in staging is the one that reaches production, never a re-build from source at deploy time. A re- build introduces the possibility that the artifact running in production was never actually the one that passed the tests.
workflow: Concretely, on a platform like GitHub Actions (which fits naturally with the AgentPlatform repo once it's pushed to GitHub per the blueprint), the workflow is defined declaratively in a YAML file at `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`:
`on: push / pull_request` defines the trigger — e.g. any push to `main`, or any PR opened against it.
`jobs:` defines one or more jobs that can run in parallel or be chained with `needs:`.
Each job specifies `runs-on:` (the runner image, e.g. `ubuntu-latest`) and a list of `steps:`.
Steps call reusable `actions` (e.g. `actions/checkout@v4`, `actions/setup-node@v4`) or raw shell commands.
Secrets (like the Vercel token or Supabase service role key) are injected via `$ {{ secrets.VERCEL_TOKEN }}`, never hardcoded in the YAML.
On success, a deploy step calls the Vercel CLI or the Vercel GitHub integration to promote the build.
On failure at any step, the workflow halts, the commit is marked with a red X in GitHub, and the developer is notified before anything reaches users.

For infrastructure-flavored automation — the kind more relevant to the Rocky Linux and Windows Server VMs in the home lab — the same shape applies but with Ansible playbooks or PowerShell DSC scripts as the deployable artifact, and a runner that has network reach to the target servers instead of to a cloud platform.
enterprise: CI/CD sits at the intersection of Layer 7 (Automation) and application delivery, but it touches nearly every layer already covered: it consumes Git (Layer 7, Session 107) as its source of truth, it depends on the OS and container layers (Layers 2 and 8) to actually run builds, it interacts with DNS and load balancers (Layer 3/5) when promoting traffic to a new version, and it is governed by change management and governance processes (Layer 10) in mature enterprises.

In a regulated financial-services-adjacent environment like FundedNext, CI/CD pipelines are often the single most audited piece of automation, because every production change traces back to a pipeline run, a commit, and an approver — which is exactly the audit trail that manual FTP-style deployments never provided.
dependencies: Version control (Git) — there is no CI/CD without a trigger source; the pipeline is defined by what happens after a commit.
A runner/compute layer — physical or virtual machines, or container orchestration, to actually execute build and test jobs.
Secrets management — pipelines need credentials (cloud tokens, database passwords, signing keys) without ever exposing them in logs or code.
Artifact storage — a registry or storage layer to hold build outputs (container registries, Vercel's build cache, npm registries).
Networking — runners need outbound access to package registries (npm, PyPI) and inbound/outbound access to deployment targets.
A test suite — a pipeline with no tests is just automated deployment, not CI/CD in the sense that catches regressions.
dependents: Once a CI/CD pipeline exists, several higher-order practices become possible for the first time:
Infrastructure as Code (Session 109) relies on a pipeline to plan and apply changes safely with peer review.
Automation Pipelines (Session 113) generalize the CI/CD pattern beyond application code to any repeatable operational task.
Blue-green and canary deployments depend on CI/CD's ability to deploy a new version alongside the old one and shift traffic gradually.
Automated rollback strategies depend on every deployment being versioned and reproducible, which only a pipeline guarantees.
Compliance and audit reporting (Layer 10) depend on the pipeline's logs as the system of record for "who changed what, when, and how it was verified."
security: A CI/CD pipeline is a high-value attack target precisely because it has broad, trusted access — to source code, to secrets, and to production systems. Key protections:
Principle of least privilege for pipeline service accounts: a deploy token should only be able to deploy, not read every secret in the vault.
Secrets are injected at runtime from a vault (never committed to the repository or hardcoded in workflow YAML).
Branch protection rules require passing checks and at least one review before merge to `main`, preventing a single compromised or careless commit from reaching production unreviewed.
Supply-chain hardening: pin third-party GitHub Actions to a commit SHA rather than a floating tag, since a tag can be silently repointed to malicious code.
Ephemeral runners (spun up per job, destroyed after) limit the blast radius if a runner is compromised mid-build.
Signed commits and signed artifacts let downstream systems verify that a build actually came from the pipeline and wasn't tampered with in transit.

example: Applied directly to Sheikh's own environment: the AgentPlatform Next.js rebuild blueprint calls for pushing the project to GitHub and importing it into Vercel. Vercel's GitHub integration is itself a CI/CD pipeline — every push to a feature branch gets an automatic preview deployment with its own URL, every merge to `main` triggers a production build and deploy, and every pull request shows the preview link directly in GitHub. This is Continuous Deployment in its purest consumer-friendly form: no YAML to hand-write for the basic flow, but the same underlying stages (build, test via `next build` type- checking, deploy, verify) are all present.

A more traditional enterprise example: a bank's core switch configuration changes are pushed through a pipeline that runs Cisco config syntax validation, a simulated deployment against a GNS3 or virtual lab topology (mirroring exactly the kind of lab Sheikh already runs), and only then applies the change to production switches during an approved maintenance window — CI/CD principles applied to network infrastructure, not just application code.
cloud: Every major cloud and SaaS platform now offers CI/CD as a managed service rather than something to build from scratch: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, AWS CodePipeline, Azure DevOps Pipelines, and Vercel's own build system. The shift is from "install and maintain a Jenkins server" to "describe your pipeline in YAML and let the platform run it on demand," which removes an entire category of infrastructure (patching Jenkins, scaling build agents) that used to be its own maintenance burden.

The tradeoff is vendor lock-in at the workflow syntax level — a GitHub Actions workflow file doesn't run unmodified on GitLab — but the underlying stage concepts (trigger, build, test, deploy, verify) transfer directly, which is why understanding the concept matters more than memorizing one vendor's YAML syntax.
automation: CI/CD is, in a real sense, the automation layer eating its own deployment process. It is worth distinguishing from plain scripting: a bash script that runs `npm run build && scp dist/ server:` is automation, but it is not CI/CD, because it has no independent trigger, no test gate, no artifact versioning, and no rollback path. CI/CD formalizes automation into a governed, observable, repeatable system — which is exactly why Layer 7 places it after PowerShell, Bash, Python, Git, REST APIs, and Infrastructure as Code: CI/CD is the layer that orchestrates all of those tools together into one coherent delivery process.
career: CI/CD literacy is one of the highest-leverage skills for the CCNA → PCNSA → RHCSA path Sheikh is on, because it is the connective tissue between traditional infrastructure roles and modern DevOps/Platform Engineering roles — the direction most European IT master's programs and job markets are actively hiring for. A Red Hat-certified engineer (RHCSA) who can also write a working GitHub Actions pipeline is materially more employable than one who can only administer a server by hand.

For the specific goal of relocating to Germany or Scandinavia for a Master's in IT/Information Systems, CI/CD experience — even lab-scale, even from a single real project like the AgentPlatform rebuild — is exactly the kind of concrete, demonstrable project work that strengthens both a CV and a study-abroad application portfolio, because it shows applied engineering judgment, not just certification study.
interview: Q: What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?

A: Continuous Delivery automatically builds and stages every change so it is always release-ready, but a human approves the final push to production. Continuous Deployment removes that human gate — anything that passes all automated checks goes to production automatically.
Q: Why should secrets never be hardcoded into a pipeline YAML file?

A: Because the YAML is stored in version control and often visible to every contributor and every fork; hardcoded secrets get exposed in commit history permanently, even if later removed, and can leak through build logs.
Q: What does "build once, deploy many" mean and why does it matter?

A: It means the exact artifact that passed testing in staging is the same binary/package promoted to production, never rebuilt from source at deploy time — this guarantees that what was tested is what actually runs, eliminating an entire class of environment-drift bugs.
Q: How would you design a rollback strategy for a CI/CD pipeline?

A: Keep every deployed artifact versioned and retained; maintain the ability to redeploy the previous known-good artifact with one command or click, without needing to rebuild it; pair this with automated health checks that can trigger rollback automatically if error rates spike after a deploy.
misconceptions: "CI/CD means fully automatic deployment with no human involved." — False for Continuous Delivery, which keeps a human approval gate by design; only Continuous Deployment is fully automatic.
"CI/CD is only for web applications." — False; the same pipeline pattern applies to network configuration, infrastructure provisioning, database migrations, and even documentation publishing.
"Passing CI means the code is bug-free." — False; CI only proves the code passes the tests that were written. Untested code paths can still ship broken.
"Setting up CI/CD is a one-time task." — False; pipelines need ongoing maintenance as dependencies, runners, and security requirements evolve.
anchors: CI = merge + build + test, early and often. CD = package + stage + (approve or auto) + release.
"Build once, deploy many" — never rebuild the artifact between staging and production.
Vercel's GitHub integration on the AgentPlatform rebuild is Continuous Deployment happening automatically, right now, without hand-written YAML.
A pipeline with no tests is not CI/CD — it's just automated deployment.
connections: CI/CD directly consumes Git (Session 107) as its trigger source and REST APIs (Session 108) as the mechanism most CI providers use to communicate with cloud platforms like Vercel and Supabase. It builds on Infrastructure as Code (Session 109) and Configuration Management (Session 110) by providing the execution engine that actually runs `terraform apply` or an Ansible playbook safely and repeatably. It sets up the next two sessions directly: Secrets Management (112) is the missing piece this session flagged repeatedly — pipelines need credentials without exposing them — and Automation Pipelines (113) generalizes everything covered here beyond just code deployment. It also reaches back to to Layer 8 Containers, since most modern CI/CD pipelines build and ship container images (Session 114 onward).

lab: Home lab exercise, mapped to existing tools (VMware Workstation Pro, Rocky Linux VM, GitHub account):
13.Create a small Node.js or Python "hello world" repo and push it to a new GitHub repository.
14.Add a `.github/workflows/ci.yml` that triggers on push, checks out the code, installs dependencies, and runs a basic test (even a placeholder `echo "tests pass"` to start).
15.Push a change and watch the Actions tab in GitHub run the job in real time — this is the CI half.

16.Extend the workflow with a second job that only runs `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` and deploys (for practice, this can simply SCP or rsync a file to the Rocky Linux VM using an SSH key stored as a GitHub secret) — this is the CD half.
17.Intentionally break a test and push again; confirm the deploy job never runs because the pipeline fails fast.

18.Optional extension: repeat this exercise against the real AgentPlatform repository once it exists on GitHub, using Vercel's native integration instead of hand-written deploy steps, and compare the two approaches.
